sources.title: Victoria and Albert Museum, The arts of the Mughal Empire
sources.note: Directly read institutional account, including founding, Humayun’s displacement, translation workshops, and Jahangir’s traveling court. Do not repeat the page’s erroneous identification of Razmnama as Ramayana.

sources.title: The Met, The Art of the Mughals before 1600
sources.note: Directly read historical and artistic account, especially 1555 restoration, Akbar’s territorial consolidation and interreligious discussions.

sources.title: The Met, South Asia, 1400 to 1600 A.D., chronology
sources.note: Official indexed original chronology checked: Suris 1540 to 1555 and 1526 event discussion on Mughal interruption and restoration.

sources.title: Marika Sardar, The Art of the Mughals after 1600, The Met
sources.note: Directly read sequence of rulers, 1739 raid, British protection and dispersal of artists to regional courts. No blanket claim that art disappeared under Aurangzeb.

sources.title: NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part II, Peasants, Zamindars and the State
sources.note: Official indexed original pages 196, 199, 206 and 207 read in full relevant excerpts: agrarian revenue, primary Baburnama irrigation passage, women’s labor and petitions. Direct PDF fetch/download failed; indexed original witness is available by exact title/page queries.

sources.title: Ruby Lal interview, Vagabond Princess: A Conversation, Yale University Press, 2024
sources.note: Directly read historian’s account of her manuscript research: Gulbadan’s family relationships, Persian prose chronicle and pilgrimage. This is researcher testimony, not a claim to have read the entire original memoir.

sources.title: Aga Khan Development Network, Walled City of Lahore Conservation
sources.note: Directly read project’s primary conservation report: Shahi Hammam, excavated hypocaust and drains; Wazir Khan Mosque entrance shops for calligraphers and bookbinders.

sources.title: Aga Khan Trust for Culture, 2008 Lisbon exhibition catalogue, School Courtyard with Boys Reading and Writing, p. 184
sources.note: Full indexed original catalogue entry checked: AKM 00288, folio 149r in this catalogue, Lahore circa 1595, ascribed to Khem Karan. Another catalogue alternates 149v/149r; public copy omits folio side. Direct PDF fetch failed. Painting interpreted as a representation, not a photograph or national enrollment statistic.

sources.title: A. Chattopadhyay, Jahangir’s interest in public health and medicine, Bulletin of the Indian Institute of History of Medicine, 1995
sources.note: Directly read author’s abstract in PubMed: memoir’s tenth accession order called for free hospitals and physicians. Card distinguishes an imperial order from proven universal implementation. No remedy efficacy claims.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal
sources.note: Directly read Outstanding Universal Value: main mausoleum construction 1632 to 1648, additional complex completed 1653; inlay, garden plan and actual tomb chamber distinguished from cenotaphs.

sources.title: The Met, Pierced Window Screen (Jali), accession 1993.67.2
sources.note: Directly read object record: second half sixteenth century, carved red sandstone, weathering suggests an exterior window. Ignore the curatorial typo giving Akbar’s accession as 1550.

sources.title: The Met, Mansur, Red-Headed Vulture and Long-Billed Vulture, accession 55.121.10.12
sources.note: Directly read object description. Bird painting circa 1615 to 1620; calligraphy on the other side older. Ornithological accuracy distinguished from imagined rocky setting.

sources.title: The Met, Mu’min Jahangir, Inkpot of the Emperor Jahangir, accession 29.145.2
sources.note: Directly read dated object and curatorial description: 1028 AH/1618 to 1619 CE, nephrite and gold, broad heavy balanced form. No hidden inscription used without direct witness.

sources.title: Louvre, Portrait of Jahangir holding a portrait of Akbar, OA 3676 B Recto
sources.note: Directly read catalogue original Persian, transliteration and French translation. Sample عمل نادر الزمان comes from the third inscription, on the green globe held by Akbar, not the explicitly later frame inscription. English translation renders peint par Nadir al-Zaman. Painting dated 1600 to 1615; catalogue does not independently date every inscription or certify artist handwriting.

sources.title: National Army Museum, Decisive events of the Indian Rebellion
sources.note: Directly read Delhi timeline and political changes: 1857 capture, trial/exile and British Crown takeover. Its phrase linking dynasty end to Zafar’s 1862 death is not used as a date for continuing Mughal government.

sources.title: Friends of the British Library Newsletter, winter 2012, Mughal India exhibition
sources.note: Original institutional PDF read; exhibition article explicitly dates British imprisonment and exile to Burma to 1858. Used with 1857 capture source to avoid conflating the two years.

proposedOverrides.name: Mughal Empire
proposedOverrides.summary: A South Asian imperial dynasty founded in 1526, with diverse peoples and influential arts.

batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Actual decoded features cover 1530 to 1783 in coarse multi-decade snapshots. Identical 1530 and 1600 bounds, the Sur interruption, and the broad final 1715 to 1783 outline are not proof of continuous effective control. Public overview warns of these limits. No unsupported successor map link added.
batchIdentityNotes.ending: 1857 capture and effective court overthrow distinguished from 1858 trial/exile and Crown takeover. The optional 1857 to 1858 phase uses exclusive upper end for the event year.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Original Persian fragment from Louvre third inscription, not explicitly later frame inscription. Catalogue verifies transcription and translated attribution, but not the artist’s own handwriting.
